title: FSSAI Suspends Licences of Two West Bengal Food Firms Over Hygiene Violations
meta_description: FSSAI suspends the licences of Kailash Formulation and Sanecure Water Project in South 24 Parganas after inspections found serious hygiene lapses.
court: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
case_name: FSSAI enforcement action against Kailash Formulation and Sanecure Water Project
citation: FSSAI licence suspension orders, South 24 Parganas, reported 6 September 2026
body: An enforcement drive in South 24 Parganas gave FSSAI inspectors a look inside two food businesses that, on paper, had nothing obviously in common beyond being licensed under the same Act. One made formulations, the other handled water. Both ended up losing their licences the same week, for reasons that read like a checklist of exactly what a food safety inspection is designed to catch.

At Kailash Formulation, inspectors found the overall cleaning, hygiene and sanitation of the premises unsatisfactory, and the firm could not produce mandatory documents it was required to maintain under its licence. Neither finding on its own is unusual in isolated enforcement actions, but together they point to a business that had let basic compliance slide on more than one front at the same time, which is typically what tips an inspection from a warning into a suspension.

Sanecure Water Project's problems were more visibly physical. Inspectors recorded pest infestation and rust on equipment used in the business, along with inadequate pest-proofing of the premises generally. For a water business specifically, pest presence and corroded equipment are not cosmetic defects; they go directly to whether the product leaving the facility is fit for consumption, which is the core question any food safety regulator is tasked with answering before it allows an operation to keep running.

Neither firm's violations were the kind that a quick fix on the day of inspection could have resolved. Missing mandatory documents at Kailash Formulation point to a gap in record-keeping that typically builds up over months of licence operation, not a one-off oversight, while rusted equipment and an active pest presence at Sanecure Water Project reflect physical conditions on the shop floor that inspectors would expect to see worsen gradually rather than appear overnight. Regulators reading an inspection report of this kind tend to treat it as evidence of a pattern rather than an isolated lapse, which is part of why suspension, rather than a lighter notice, followed so quickly in both cases.

FSSAI responded to both sets of findings by suspending each firm's licence with immediate effect. News coverage of the action used the word cancellation loosely in some headlines, but the underlying reporting describes a suspension rather than an outright cancellation, a distinction the Food Safety and Standards Act treats as meaningfully different. Suspension is the regulator's intermediate tool, used where the violations found are serious enough to justify stopping operations immediately but where the business still has the chance to correct the problems and seek restoration of its licence.

The broader regulatory framework around these actions is worth keeping in mind for any food business operator worried about a similar visit. An improvement notice ordinarily comes first for correctable defects, and the statutory period given for corrective measures under such a notice cannot ordinarily be less than fourteen days. Suspension is the step taken when the violations are not the kind an improvement notice can safely wait out, and FSSAI's own regulations require that the operator still be given a reasonable opportunity to be heard before a suspension order takes effect.

For operators running multiple sites or multiple categories of food business under one umbrella, the pairing of these two cases in the same enforcement sweep is a reminder that hygiene lapses and missing documentation are treated as independently sufficient grounds for suspension, not as problems that need to occur together to attract action. A business that keeps its paperwork in order but lets pest control slip, or one that controls pests well but cannot produce the records its licence requires, is equally exposed. Both strands of compliance, physical conditions on the shop floor and the documentary trail behind them, have to hold up at the same time for a licence to stay safe from suspension.

Routine enforcement drives of this kind rarely get the same attention as a single high-profile recall, yet they account for a large share of the licence actions FSSAI and state food safety bodies take across the country in any given month. Small and mid-sized manufacturers, in particular, tend to underestimate how quickly a documentation gap or a pest-control lapse can escalate into a suspension once an inspector is actually on the premises, since the regulator's threshold for acting does not depend on the scale of the business or how long it has operated without incident before that visit.
why_it_matters: Food business operators should treat hygiene and sanitation failures and missing mandatory documentation as independently sufficient grounds for an FSSAI suspension, since either alone was enough to trigger action against these two firms. Operators facing an inspection should expect suspension, not just an improvement notice, where pest infestation, equipment condition or documentation gaps are serious, and should know they are entitled to a hearing before a suspension order takes effect.
card_summary: FSSAI suspends the licences of two South 24 Parganas food firms, Kailash Formulation and Sanecure Water Project, after inspections found hygiene failures, missing records and pest infestation.
card_tip: Treat hygiene violations and missing mandatory licence documentation as separate, independently sufficient grounds for an FSSAI suspension; fixing one without the other still leaves a licence exposed.
verification_notes: The identities of both firms, their location in South 24 Parganas, the specific violations found at each (unsatisfactory hygiene and missing documents at Kailash Formulation; pest infestation and rusted equipment at Sanecure Water Project), and the suspension of both licences are confirmed across Outlook Business, ETV Bharat and The Print, all reporting on or about 6 September 2026. Headlines calling the action a cancellation are noted as inconsistent with the suspension described in the body of the same reports, and this article follows the more specific description of a suspension.
